qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Pictorial (monocular) cues explain painted depth.

qa.q: Case: A doctor asks a patient to look at a pen moving towards her nose and watches the eyes turn inward. Which cue is being demonstrated?
qa.e: Eyes turning inward for near objects is convergence.

qa.q: Perceiving a person walking away as the same size, though the retinal image shrinks, is
qa.e: Perceived size stays stable with distance.

qa.q: A door that opens towards you casts a trapezium-shaped image but is still seen as rectangular. This is
qa.e: Shape is perceived as stable despite angle.

qa.q: White chalk looks white both in bright sunlight and in a dim classroom because of
qa.e: Relative brightness is perceived as constant.

qa.q: Perceptual constancy refers to
qa.a: perceiving objects as relatively stable despite changes in their retinal images
qa.e: Constancy gives a stable world.

qa.q: Which constancy explains why a dinner plate seen from the side, casting an oval image, is still seen as round?
qa.e: Angle changes the image, not the perceived shape.

qa.q: Brightness constancy occurs because
qa.a: an object reflects the same proportion of light under different illumination
qa.e: The ratio of reflected light stays the same relative to surroundings.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A friend standing far away in a playground is not perceived as a small child. Reason (R): The retinal image of a distant friend stays exactly the same size as when she is near.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true (size constancy); R is false because the retinal image shrinks with distance.

qa.q: Case: In a dim cinema hall, Anu still perceives her white kurta as white, not grey. Which process is responsible?
qa.e: Perceived brightness remains constant under changed lighting.

qa.q: An illusion is
qa.a: a misperception of a real stimulus
qa.e: The stimulus exists but is perceived incorrectly.

qa.q: The Muller-Lyer illusion is an example of a
qa.e: It involves misjudging line lengths.

qa.q: In the Muller-Lyer illusion, the line that appears longer is the one with
qa.e: Outward fins make the line look longer.

qa.q: The phi phenomenon refers to
qa.a: perceiving movement when stationary lights flash in quick succession
qa.e: It is an apparent-movement illusion.

qa.q: Why do we see smooth motion in a cinema film?
qa.a: Because of apparent movement (phi phenomenon) from rapidly shown still frames
qa.e: Rapid succession of frames creates apparent motion.

qa.q: How does an illusion differ from a hallucination?
qa.a: An illusion involves a real stimulus misperceived; a hallucination occurs without a real stimulus
qa.e: The presence of a real stimulus is the key difference.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Most people experience the Muller-Lyer illusion. Reason (R): Many illusions are universal and persist even when we know the lines are equal.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Their universal, persistent nature explains why most people experience it.

qa.q: Case: In an activity, students draw two equal 8 cm lines, add outward fins to one and inward arrowheads to the other, then ask classmates which is longer. What are they most likely to hear?
qa.a: The line with outward fins looks longer
qa.e: That is the typical Muller-Lyer effect.

qa.q: Who studied cross-cultural differences in susceptibility to visual illusions?
qa.e: They conducted the classic cross-cultural illusion studies.

qa.q: The 'carpentered world' refers to
qa.a: environments full of rectangular shapes, straight lines and right angles
qa.e: Built environments with many right angles.

qa.q: According to the carpentered-world idea, who is likely to be more susceptible to the Muller-Lyer illusion?
qa.a: People raised among rectangular buildings and furniture
qa.e: Experience with corners makes fins look like depth cues.

qa.q: Cross-cultural studies of illusions show that perception is
qa.a: influenced by cultural and ecological experience
qa.e: Experience shapes perception.

qa.q: A person unfamiliar with pictures may have difficulty in
qa.a: interpreting depth cues in a 2-D drawing
qa.e: Reading pictorial depth is partly learned.

qa.q: Why might a health poster with perspective drawings be misread in some communities?
qa.a: People with little exposure to such pictures may not read the depth cues as intended
qa.e: Pictorial conventions are learned through experience.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Susceptibility to the Muller-Lyer illusion differs across cultural groups. Reason (R): The environment people grow up in shapes how they interpret angles and lines.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Different environments explain different susceptibility.

qa.q: Case: An NGO finds that villagers interpret a poster's 'far away' figure as a 'small person' rather than a distant one. This finding supports the idea that
qa.a: pictorial depth perception depends on cultural experience
qa.e: Reading pictorial depth is shaped by exposure to pictures.

qa.q: Learning is best defined as
qa.a: a relatively permanent change in behaviour or behavioural potential due to experience or practice
qa.e: Experience-based and relatively permanent are the key words.

qa.q: Which is NOT an example of learning?
qa.a: A teenager's voice becoming deeper at puberty
qa.e: Voice change is due to maturation.

qa.q: Why are changes due to fatigue not considered learning?
qa.a: They are temporary and do not result from practice
qa.e: Fatigue effects disappear after rest.

qa.q: Learning is said to be 'inferred' because
qa.a: it cannot be observed directly and is judged from changes in performance
qa.e: We infer learning from performance.

qa.q: In studying learning, a pre-test, practice and a post-test are used to show that learning
qa.a: is a process involving a sequence of events
qa.e: Learning unfolds over a sequence of psychological events.

qa.q: A baby walking at about one year without any training is an example of
qa.e: Walking emerges on a genetic timetable.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Changes in behaviour caused by drugs are not learning. Reason (R): Drug effects are usually temporary and are not produced by practice.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The reason given is exactly why they don't qualify as learning.

qa.q: Case: After a motorbike accident, Rahul limps for six months. Is his limp an example of learning?
qa.a: No, because it results from injury, not experience or practice
qa.e: Injury-caused changes are excluded from learning.

qa.q: Who first demonstrated classical conditioning?
qa.e: Pavlov's work with dogs established classical conditioning.

qa.q: The simplest form of learning is
qa.e: Conditioning involves learning associations.

qa.q: In Pavlov's experiment, what was paired with food?
qa.e: The bell (or a similar sound) was paired with food.

qa.q: After conditioning, Pavlov's dog salivated to
qa.e: The bell alone produced salivation.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the paradigms of learning?
qa.e: Maturation is not learning.

qa.q: Classical conditioning is a form of associative learning because the organism learns
qa.e: The association between bell and food is learnt.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Pavlov's dogs began to salivate at the sound of the bell. Reason (R): The bell had been repeatedly paired with the presentation of food.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Repeated pairing created the association.

qa.q: Case: A child feels hungry whenever she hears the pressure cooker whistle, because it usually goes off just before lunch. This is most like
qa.e: A sound paired with food now triggers a response.

qa.q: In classical conditioning, the stimulus that naturally produces a response without learning is the
qa.e: The US produces the UR naturally.

qa.q: In Pavlov's experiment, salivation to the bell is the
qa.e: It is a learned response to the CS.

qa.q: Before conditioning, the bell was a
qa.e: It produced no salivation before pairing.

qa.q: Acquisition in classical conditioning refers to
qa.a: the stage in which the CR is learned through repeated CS-US pairings
qa.e: Acquisition = learning the association.

qa.q: Riya felt sick after eating at a stall and now feels nauseous when she sees its signboard. The signboard is the
qa.e: It was neutral and became linked to sickness.

qa.q: In the same example, nausea caused directly by the spoilt food is the
qa.e: Natural reaction to the US is the UR.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A neutral stimulus can come to produce a response it did not produce before. Reason (R): Through repeated pairing with an unconditioned stimulus, it becomes a conditioned stimulus.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Pairing transforms a neutral stimulus into a CS.

qa.q: Case: Every evening, Arjun's mother switches on the TV news theme just before serving dinner. Now Arjun feels hungry on hearing the theme even at noon. Identify the CR.
qa.a: Feeling hungry on hearing the theme
qa.e: The learned response to the CS (theme) is the CR.

qa.q: Which time relation between CS and US is the most effective for classical conditioning?
qa.e: In delayed conditioning, the CS starts first and overlaps the US.

qa.q: When the US is presented before the CS, the procedure is called
qa.e: US first = backward.

qa.q: In trace conditioning,
qa.a: the CS begins and ends before the US is presented
qa.e: Only a memory trace of the CS remains when the US arrives.

qa.q: An electric shock used as a US is
qa.e: Painful stimuli are aversive.

qa.q: Which procedure is the least effective for producing a conditioned response?
qa.e: When the US comes first, the CS predicts nothing.

qa.q: A louder bell (more intense CS) compared with a soft bell usually results in
qa.e: Intensity of CS speeds acquisition.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Delayed conditioning is the most effective procedure. Reason (R): In delayed conditioning, the onset of the CS signals that the US is about to come.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the CS reliably predicts the US, R explains A.

qa.q: Case: In a study, a tone sounds and stops; 10 seconds later a puff of air hits the eye. Which time relation is used?
qa.e: The CS ends before the US starts.

qa.q: Operant conditioning was first investigated by
qa.e: Skinner studied operant behaviour.

qa.q: Operants are
qa.a: voluntary behaviours controlled by their consequences
qa.e: Operants operate on the environment and depend on consequences.

qa.q: In the Skinner box, the food pellet acts as a
qa.e: Food strengthens lever pressing.

qa.q: Operant conditioning is also called instrumental conditioning because
qa.a: the response is instrumental in obtaining the reward
qa.e: The behaviour is a means to the outcome.

qa.q: Reinforcement is any event that
qa.a: increases the likelihood of the response it follows
qa.e: By definition, reinforcement strengthens a response.

qa.q: The key difference between classical and operant conditioning is that in operant conditioning
qa.a: voluntary responses are shaped by their consequences
qa.e: Operant = consequences of voluntary behaviour.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The rat in the Skinner box presses the lever more often over time. Reason (R): Lever pressing is followed by food, which reinforces the response.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Reinforcement explains the increase.

qa.q: Case: A shy student begins to raise her hand more often after her teacher warmly praises every attempt she makes. This is
qa.e: Voluntary behaviour increases due to a pleasant consequence.

qa.q: Which is a secondary reinforcer?
qa.e: Money's value is learned.

qa.q: A response that removes an unpleasant stimulus is strengthened through
qa.e: Removing the aversive stimulus reinforces the response.

qa.q: Which of these is a primary reinforcer?
qa.e: Food satisfies a biological need.

qa.q: What is the effect of delaying reinforcement after a response?
qa.e: Immediate reinforcement works best.

qa.q: A rat learns faster when given three food pellets per press instead of one. This shows the effect of
qa.e: Larger reinforcement speeds learning.

qa.q: You switch off a screeching alarm by pressing a button, and you learn to press it quickly. The screeching alarm is a
qa.e: An unpleasant stimulus whose removal strengthens behaviour is a negative reinforcer.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Praise from parents can strengthen a child's behaviour. Reason (R): Praise is a primary reinforcer that satisfies a biological need.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false because praise is a secondary (learned) reinforcer.

qa.q: Case: A coaching institute gives toppers a certificate six months after the test, and finds it does little to motivate students. The most likely reason is
qa.e: Delayed reinforcement weakens its effect.

qa.q: Reinforcing a response after a fixed number of responses is a
qa.e: Ratio = number of responses; fixed = constant.

qa.q: Receiving a salary on the last day of every month is an example of a
qa.e: Reward is tied to a fixed time period.

qa.q: Which schedule is illustrated by slot machines and lotteries?
qa.e: Rewards follow an unpredictable number of responses.

qa.q: Behaviour learned under partial reinforcement, compared with continuous reinforcement, is
qa.e: Intermittent rewards make the response persist.

qa.q: A teacher who gives surprise tests at unpredictable times is using a
qa.e: Reinforcement opportunities come after unpredictable time periods.

qa.q: For teaching a brand-new behaviour quickly, the best schedule is usually
qa.e: Rewarding every correct response speeds early learning.

qa.q: Assertion (A): People keep checking their phones for messages many times a day. Reason (R): Messages arrive after unpredictable time periods, which acts like a variable interval schedule.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Variable schedules sustain persistent checking.

qa.q: Case: A garment worker is paid ₹50 for every 5 shirts stitched. If she stitches 35 shirts in a day, how much does she earn?
qa.e: On this fixed ratio schedule, pay = (35 ÷ 5) × ₹50.

qa.q: Negative reinforcement
qa.a: strengthens a response by removing an unpleasant stimulus
qa.e: Negative reinforcement increases behaviour; punishment decreases it.

qa.q: Punishment refers to
qa.a: an aversive stimulus following a response that decreases the response
qa.e: Punishment suppresses behaviour.

qa.q: Opening an umbrella when it starts raining is an example of
qa.e: The aversive situation (rain) is already present and the response ends it.

qa.q: Leaving home early to avoid being caught in a traffic jam is
qa.e: The response prevents the aversive event from occurring.

qa.q: Which is the correct difference between negative reinforcement and punishment?
qa.a: Negative reinforcement increases a behaviour; punishment decreases it
qa.e: Their effects on behaviour are opposite.

qa.q: A child stops touching the stove after getting a mild burn. This is an example of
qa.e: The aversive consequence decreased the behaviour.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Negative reinforcement is a type of punishment. Reason (R): Both negative reinforcement and punishment involve aversive stimuli.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false (negative reinforcement strengthens behaviour, punishment weakens it); R is true since both involve aversive stimuli.

qa.q: Case: Manish has a headache, takes a balm that relieves it, and now uses the balm sooner whenever a headache starts. His use of the balm has been strengthened by
qa.e: Removal of the painful headache strengthens the behaviour.

qa.q: When a conditioned response gradually disappears because reinforcement is withheld, it is called
qa.e: Without reinforcement, the response weakens.

qa.q: After extinction and a period of rest, a conditioned response reappears when the CS is presented. This is
qa.e: The response returns after rest.

qa.q: A child who fears a doctor in a white coat also fears a laboratory technician in a white coat. This is
qa.e: A similar stimulus produces the same response.

qa.q: Stimulus discrimination means
qa.e: It is the opposite of generalisation.

qa.q: Reinforcing successive approximations to a desired behaviour is called
qa.e: Shaping rewards small steps towards the target.

qa.q: Teaching a dog a trick in which it must first fetch a ball, then drop it, then sit, each step leading to the next, uses
qa.e: Linking responses into a sequence is chaining.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A child stops throwing tantrums when parents consistently stop giving attention to them. Reason (R): Extinction occurs when the reinforcer that maintained a behaviour is withdrawn.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Attention was the reinforcer; withdrawing it leads to extinction.

qa.q: Case: A baby calls every man 'Papa'. Later, she uses the word only for her father. The change shows
qa.e: She first generalised, then learned to discriminate.

qa.q: Who conducted the Bobo doll experiment on observational learning?
qa.e: Bandura is known for social/observational learning.

qa.q: Observational learning is also known as
qa.e: It involves learning from models.

qa.q: In Bandura's study, which group of children showed the least aggression in the free-play session?
qa.a: Those who saw the model punished
qa.e: Seeing punishment reduced the performance of aggression.

qa.q: When all children were later offered rewards for imitating the model,
qa.a: all of them showed aggressive behaviour
qa.e: This showed learning had occurred in every group.

qa.q: The key conclusion of the Bobo doll study is that
qa.a: behaviour can be learned by watching, even without being performed or reinforced directly
qa.e: Learning and performance are different.

qa.q: A teenager copies the hairstyle of a popular cricketer. This is an example of
qa.e: Imitating a model is observational learning.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Children may become more aggressive after watching violent shows in which violence is rewarded. Reason (R): Through observational learning, people learn behaviours modelled by others and their consequences.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Observing rewarded aggression teaches it.

qa.q: Case: A new employee notices that colleagues who speak up in meetings get praised by the manager, so she starts speaking up too. Her behaviour is best explained by
qa.e: She learned from models' consequences.

qa.q: Insight learning was demonstrated by
qa.e: Kohler studied chimpanzees solving problems.

qa.q: A key feature of insight learning is that
qa.a: the solution appears suddenly and can be transferred to similar problems
qa.e: Insight is sudden and generalisable.

qa.q: Latent learning means
qa.a: learning that occurs without reinforcement and is not shown until there is a reason
qa.e: Learning stays hidden until needed.

qa.q: Tolman's rats explored a maze without food and later ran quickly to the food once it was introduced. This shows they had formed a
qa.e: A mental map of the maze guided them.

qa.q: Cognitive learning differs from conditioning mainly because it involves
qa.e: The learner's mental representations change.

qa.q: The chimpanzee in Kohler's studies is famous by the name
qa.e: Sultan joined sticks to reach bananas.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A rat that explored a maze without reward can find food quickly when food is introduced. Reason (R): Learning had taken place during exploration in the form of a cognitive map.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The hidden map explains the quick performance.

qa.q: Case: After struggling with a jigsaw, Asha stops, stares at it, and suddenly sees that the sky pieces fit at the bottom because the picture is upside down. Later she solves similar puzzles quickly. This is
qa.e: Sudden solution that transfers is insight.

qa.q: Ebbinghaus used nonsense syllables because
qa.a: they reduce the influence of prior meaning and associations
qa.e: Nonsense syllables give a cleaner measure of learning.

qa.q: Learning Spanish words along with their English meanings is an example of
qa.e: Each word is paired with another.

qa.q: In paired-associates learning, the first member of each pair is called the
qa.e: First = stimulus term; second = response term.

qa.q: Learning the steps of CPR in their exact sequence is
qa.e: Order matters in serial learning.

qa.q: In free recall, which items are usually recalled best?
qa.a: Those at the beginning and the end of the list
qa.e: Beginning and end items have an advantage.

qa.q: Recalling words from a mixed list category by category (fruits, then animals) shows
qa.e: Grouping by category during recall is clustering.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A list of 30 nonsense syllables takes more trials to learn than a list of 10. Reason (R): Ebbinghaus used nonsense syllables in his experiments.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the use of nonsense syllables doesn't explain the effect; list length does.

qa.q: Case: In a class activity, students learn a list of 12 meaningful words and a list of 12 nonsense syllables. Which result is expected?
qa.a: The meaningful list is learned in fewer trials
qa.e: Meaningfulness speeds verbal learning.

qa.q: Which psychologist described three phases of skill learning?
qa.e: Fitts proposed cognitive, associative and autonomous phases.

qa.q: The correct sequence of Fitts's phases is
qa.e: Understanding → linking steps → automatic performance.

qa.q: In the autonomous phase of skill learning,
qa.a: performance becomes automatic and needs little attention
qa.e: The skill runs smoothly with little effort.

qa.q: Learning a subject purely because one finds it interesting reflects
qa.e: Interest and enjoyment are intrinsic.

qa.q: Preparedness for learning refers to
qa.a: species-specific biological readiness to learn certain associations
qa.e: Some associations are learned easily due to biology.

qa.q: Why is feedback important in skill learning?
qa.a: It tells the learner how well they are doing so errors can be corrected
qa.e: Knowledge of results guides improvement.

qa.q: Assertion (A): An experienced driver can talk while driving. Reason (R): In the autonomous phase, a skill needs little conscious attention.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Automaticity frees attention, explaining A.

qa.q: Case: Learning to dislike a food after getting sick from it once is quick, but learning to dislike it after a mild shock is slow. This difference is best explained by
qa.e: Organisms are biologically ready to link taste with sickness.

qa.q: A learning disability involves difficulties in reading, writing, speaking or maths in a child who
qa.e: The difficulty is specific despite normal intelligence.

qa.q: Which of these is one of the most common learning disabilities?
qa.e: Dyslexia, a difficulty with reading and spelling, is one of the most common learning disabilities; ADHD, autism and colour blindness are not learning disabilities.

qa.q: Which is a common sign of a learning disability?
qa.a: Reading 'was' as 'saw' and confusing similar letters
qa.e: Reversals and confusions are typical signs.

qa.q: Learning disabilities are NOT caused by
qa.a: sensory impairment or lack of opportunity to learn
qa.e: These causes are explicitly excluded.

qa.q: The best approach for a child with a learning disability is
qa.a: early identification and remedial teaching suited to the child
qa.e: Appropriate teaching and support help.

qa.q: Which statement about children with learning disabilities is correct?
qa.a: With suitable support they can learn and achieve well
qa.e: Remedial methods help them succeed.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A child with dyslexia may do well in drawing and puzzles. Reason (R): A learning disability is specific; it does not mean low overall intelligence.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Specificity of the difficulty explains A.

qa.q: Case: A Class 4 teacher notices that Riya, who reasons well orally, writes 'p' for 'q', loses track of lines while reading, and often bumps into things. The most appropriate step is to
qa.a: discuss with parents and arrange assessment by a specialist
qa.e: Signs suggest a possible learning disability needing assessment.

qa.q: Memory is best defined as
qa.a: the process of retaining and recovering information over time
qa.e: Memory retains and recovers information over time.

qa.q: The correct order of memory stages is
qa.e: Information is recorded, kept, then brought back.

qa.q: Bringing stored information into awareness when needed is
qa.e: Retrieval = recovering stored information.

qa.q: The stage at which information is first recorded and registered in a usable form is
qa.e: Encoding converts input into a form the memory system can use.

qa.q: Forgetting can occur
qa.a: due to failure at any of the three stages
qa.e: Each stage can fail.

qa.q: Retaining encoded information over a period of time is called
qa.e: Storage keeps information available over time.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A student who did not pay attention in class may be unable to remember the lesson. Reason (R): Information that is not properly encoded cannot be stored or retrieved well.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Poor encoding leads to poor memory, explaining A.

qa.q: Case: Sana is sure she knows the capital of Australia; it comes to her an hour after the quiz ended. Her problem during the quiz was mainly at the stage of
qa.e: The information was stored (she recalled it later) but couldn't be accessed then.

qa.q: Who proposed the stage model of memory?
qa.e: Atkinson and Shiffrin proposed it in 1968.

qa.q: The three memory systems in the stage model are
qa.a: sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory
qa.e: These are the three stores.

qa.q: Which control process moves information from sensory memory into STM?
qa.e: Only attended information enters STM.

qa.q: In which year was the Atkinson-Shiffrin model proposed?
qa.e: It was proposed in 1968.

qa.q: The information-processing approach to memory is based on an analogy with
qa.e: Input, processing, storage and output are compared to computing.

qa.q: Which is a criticism of the stage model?
qa.a: It treats STM as a passive store, whereas STM is an active working space
qa.e: Working memory research showed STM is active.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rehearsal helps information stay in short-term memory. Reason (R): In the stage model, rehearsal is a control process that maintains information in STM.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: R describes rehearsal's role, explaining A.

qa.q: Case: While walking past a shop, Ravi glimpses dozens of items in the window but later can name only the cricket bat he looked at closely. In stage-model terms, this is because
qa.a: only the attended item moved from sensory memory to STM
qa.e: Attention selects what moves on to STM.

qa.q: The capacity of short-term memory is about
qa.e: Miller's 'magical number seven, plus or minus two'.

qa.q: Visual sensory memory is called
qa.e: Icon = image.

qa.q: Without rehearsal, information in STM is usually lost within
qa.e: STM duration is very short.

qa.q: Grouping the letters I-S-R-O-R-B-I-A-I-I-M-S into ISRO, RBI and AIIMS is an example of
qa.e: Chunking groups items into meaningful units.

qa.q: In Peterson and Peterson's experiment, participants counted backwards after seeing letters in order to
qa.e: Blocking rehearsal showed how quickly STM fades.

qa.q: Information in STM is encoded mainly
qa.e: STM uses sound-based codes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Repeating a phone number keeps it in STM, but it may still be forgotten after you stop. Reason (R): Maintenance rehearsal only maintains information; it does not create deep, meaningful links for LTM.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Without elaboration, transfer to LTM is weak, explaining A.

qa.q: Case: Meena learns the term 'photosynthesis' by connecting it to 'photo = light' and 'synthesis = making', and to plants in her garden. She is using
qa.e: Linking meaning with existing knowledge is elaborative rehearsal.

qa.q: Long-term memory has
qa.a: practically unlimited capacity and long duration
qa.e: LTM is vast and lasting.

qa.q: Information in LTM is encoded mainly
qa.e: LTM stores meaning.

qa.q: Who proposed the working memory model?
qa.e: Baddeley described working memory.

qa.q: Which component of working memory coordinates attention and the other components?
qa.e: The central executive is the control system.

qa.q: Repeating a telephone number silently to yourself uses the
qa.e: The phonological loop holds speech-based information.

qa.q: Picturing the layout of your house to count its windows uses the
qa.e: Visual-spatial images are held in the sketchpad.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Working memory is described as an active workspace. Reason (R): Baddeley proposed the working memory model.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but who proposed it doesn't explain why it is active; holding and manipulating information does.

qa.q: Case: Students are asked to compare the three memory stores. Which comparison is correct?
qa.a: Sensory: large capacity, very brief; STM: 7 ± 2 items, about 30 s; LTM: unlimited, long-lasting
qa.e: This is the standard comparison.

qa.q: The levels of processing approach was proposed by
qa.e: Craik and Lockhart proposed it in 1972.

qa.q: According to the levels of processing approach, the best retention results from
qa.e: Processing meaning is the deepest level.

qa.q: Noticing whether a word is written in capital or small letters is
qa.e: Physical features are processed at the structural level.

qa.q: Judging whether two words rhyme involves
qa.e: Rhyme is about sound.

qa.q: In which year did Craik and Lockhart propose the levels of processing approach?
qa.e: It was proposed in 1972.

qa.q: Which study method best uses the levels of processing idea?
qa.a: Explaining a concept in your own words with examples
qa.e: Working with meaning gives deep processing.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Students who relate new ideas to their own experience remember them better. Reason (R): Relating information to existing knowledge involves semantic, deep processing.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Deep processing explains better memory.

qa.e: Chunking forms meaningful units.

qa.q: Thinking is best described as
